claim: Most eukaryotic cells retain a mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis (FASII) pathway whose acyl carrier protein (mACP) and 4-phosphopantetheine (Ppant) prosthetic group provide a soluble scaffold for acyl chain synthesis.
source: Most eukaryotic cells retain a mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis (FASII) pathway whose acyl carrier protein (mACP) and 4-phosphopantetheine (Ppant) prosthetic group provide a soluble scaffold for acyl chain synthesis and biochemically couple FASII activity to mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) assembly and Fe-S cluster biogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about eukaryotic cell biology and mitochondrial FASII pathways.

claim: The mitochondrial FASII pathway biochemically couples FASII activity to mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) assembly and Fe-S cluster biogenesis in most eukaryotic cells.
source: Most eukaryotic cells retain a mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis (FASII) pathway whose acyl carrier protein (mACP) and 4-phosphopantetheine (Ppant) prosthetic group provide a soluble scaffold for acyl chain synthesis and biochemically couple FASII activity to mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) assembly and Fe-S cluster biogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the functional coupling of mitochondrial pathways.

claim: The mitochondrion of Plasmodium falciparum malaria parasites lacks FASII enzymes.
source: In contrast, the mitochondrion of Plasmodium falciparum malaria parasites lacks FASII enzymes yet curiously retains a divergent mACP lacking a Ppant group.
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript and by the BLAST analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum retains a divergent mACP lacking a Ppant group.
source: In contrast, the mitochondrion of Plasmodium falciparum malaria parasites lacks FASII enzymes yet curiously retains a divergent mACP lacking a Ppant group.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ligand-dependent knockdown of mACP is lethal to P. falciparum parasites.
source: We report that ligand-dependent knockdown of mACP is lethal to parasites, indicating an essential FASII-independent function.
evidence: This is supported by the growth assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: mACP has an essential FASII-independent function in P. falciparum.
source: We report that ligand-dependent knockdown of mACP is lethal to parasites, indicating an essential FASII-independent function.
evidence: This is inferred from the lethality of mACP knockdown in parasites that lack mitochondrial FASII enzymes.

claim: Decyl-ubiquinone rescues parasites temporarily from death upon mACP knockdown.
source: Decyl-ubiquinone rescues parasites temporarily from death, suggesting a dominant dysfunction of the mitochondrial ETC.
evidence: This is supported by the growth assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: mACP knockdown causes a dominant dysfunction of the mitochondrial ETC.
source: Decyl-ubiquinone rescues parasites temporarily from death, suggesting a dominant dysfunction of the mitochondrial ETC.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of decyl-ubiquinone to rescue parasites, as dQ is known to bypass ETC dysfunction.

claim: Plasmodium mACP binds and stabilizes the Isd11-Nfs1 complex required for Fe-S cluster biosynthesis.
source: Biochemical studies reveal that Plasmodium mACP binds and stabilizes the Isd11-Nfs1 complex required for Fe-S cluster biosynthesis, despite lacking the Ppant group required for this association in other eukaryotes, and knockdown of parasite mACP causes loss of Nfs1 and the Rieske Fe-S protein in ETC complex III.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP experiments (Figure 2D, 2F, 2G) and by loss of Nfs1 upon mACP knockdown (Figure 4A).

claim: Plasmodium mACP binds Isd11 despite lacking the Ppant group required for this association in other eukaryotes.
source: Biochemical studies reveal that Plasmodium mACP binds and stabilizes the Isd11-Nfs1 complex required for Fe-S cluster biosynthesis, despite lacking the Ppant group required for this association in other eukaryotes, and knockdown of parasite mACP causes loss of Nfs1 and the Rieske Fe-S protein in ETC complex III.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP experiments (Figure 2D, 2F, 2G) showing mACP-Isd11 interaction and sequence analysis showing lack of conserved Ser (Figure 1A).

claim: Knockdown of parasite mACP causes loss of Nfs1.
source: Biochemical studies reveal that Plasmodium mACP binds and stabilizes the Isd11-Nfs1 complex required for Fe-S cluster biosynthesis, despite lacking the Ppant group required for this association in other eukaryotes, and knockdown of parasite mACP causes loss of Nfs1 and the Rieske Fe-S protein in ETC complex III.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Knockdown of parasite mACP causes loss of the Rieske Fe-S protein in ETC complex III.
source: Biochemical studies reveal that Plasmodium mACP binds and stabilizes the Isd11-Nfs1 complex required for Fe-S cluster biosynthesis, despite lacking the Ppant group required for this association in other eukaryotes, and knockdown of parasite mACP causes loss of Nfs1 and the Rieske Fe-S protein in ETC complex III.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Plasmodium parasites have evolved to decouple mitochondrial Fe-S cluster biogenesis from FASII activity.
source: This work reveals that Plasmodium parasites have evolved to decouple mitochondrial Fe-S cluster biogenesis from FASII activity, and this adaptation is a shared metabolic feature of other apicomplexan pathogens, including Toxoplasma and Babesia.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of mitochondrial FASII enzymes while retaining mACP function in Fe-S cluster biogenesis.

claim: Decoupling of mitochondrial Fe-S cluster biogenesis from FASII activity is a shared metabolic feature of other apicomplexan pathogens, including Toxoplasma and Babesia.
source: This work reveals that Plasmodium parasites have evolved to decouple mitochondrial Fe-S cluster biogenesis from FASII activity, and this adaptation is a shared metabolic feature of other apicomplexan pathogens, including Toxoplasma and Babesia.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hundreds of thousands of people die from malaria each year, especially in tropical Africa.
source: Malaria is an ancient scourge of humanity and remains a pressing global health challenge, especially in tropical Africa where hundreds of thousands of people die from malaria each year.
evidence: This is a statement of established epidemiological knowledge about malaria.

claim: P. falciparum retains an essential mitochondrion required for biosynthesis of pyrimidines, acetyl-CoA, and Fe-S clusters.
source: P. falciparum retains an essential mitochondrion required for biosynthesis of pyrimidines, acetyl-CoA, and Fe-S clusters (Painter et al., 2007; Jhun et al., 2018; van Dooren et al., 2006; Oppenheim et al., 2014; Gisselberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The parasite mitochondrion contains enzymes involved in the citric acid cycle and biosynthesis of ATP and heme, but these pathways are dispensable for blood-stage parasites.
source: Although the parasite mitochondrion also contains enzymes involved in the citric acid cycle and biosynthesis of ATP and heme, these pathways are dispensable for blood-stage parasites, which can scavenge host heme and obtain sufficient ATP from cytoplasmic glycolysis (Ke et al., 2014; Nagaraj et al., 2013; Ke et al., 2015; Sturm et al., 2015; MacRae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Blood-stage parasites can scavenge host heme and obtain sufficient ATP from cytoplasmic glycolysis.
source: Although the parasite mitochondrion also contains enzymes involved in the citric acid cycle and biosynthesis of ATP and heme, these pathways are dispensable for blood-stage parasites, which can scavenge host heme and obtain sufficient ATP from cytoplasmic glycolysis (Ke et al., 2014; Nagaraj et al., 2013; Ke et al., 2015; Sturm et al., 2015; MacRae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Most eukaryotes contain a mitochondrial type II fatty acid biosynthesis (FASII) pathway that generates the octanoate precursor of the lipoic acid cofactor.
source: In addition to these pathways, most eukaryotes, including mammals and yeast, also contain a mitochondrial type II fatty acid biosynthesis (FASII) pathway that generates the octanoate precursor of the lipoic acid cofactor used by several mitochondrial dehydrogenases (Hiltunen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: FASII enzymes in P. falciparum have been lost by the mitochondrion and are retained instead by the apicoplast organelle.
source: In contrast to human and yeast cells, FASII enzymes in P. falciparum have been lost by the mitochondrion and are retained instead by the apicoplast organelle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Shears et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and by BLAST analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Critical lipoate-dependent enzymes are present in the parasite mitochondrion.
source: Although critical lipoate-dependent enzymes are present in the parasite mitochondrion (Jhun et al., 2018), prior work has shown that these enzymes utilize scavenged lipoate obtained from the red blood cell rather than de novo synthesis (Allary et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Lipoate-dependent enzymes in the parasite mitochondrion utilize scavenged lipoate obtained from the red blood cell rather than de novo synthesis.
source: Although critical lipoate-dependent enzymes are present in the parasite mitochondrion (Jhun et al., 2018), prior work has shown that these enzymes utilize scavenged lipoate obtained from the red blood cell rather than de novo synthesis (Allary et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: The acyl carrier protein (ACP) contains a strictly conserved Ser residue modified by a 4-phosphopantetheine (Ppant) group.
source: The acyl carrier protein (ACP) is a key component of FASII and contains a strictly conserved Ser residue modified by a 4-phosphopantetheine (Ppant) group whose terminal thiol tethers the nascent acyl chain during fatty acid initiation, modification, and elongation (Chan and Vogel, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work and represents established knowledge about ACP structure and function.

claim: The terminal thiol of the Ppant group tethers the nascent acyl chain during fatty acid initiation, modification, and elongation.
source: The acyl carrier protein (ACP) is a key component of FASII and contains a strictly conserved Ser residue modified by a 4-phosphopantetheine (Ppant) group whose terminal thiol tethers the nascent acyl chain during fatty acid initiation, modification, and elongation (Chan and Vogel, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work and represents established knowledge about ACP function.

claim: The P. falciparum apicoplast features a well-studied ACP homolog (PF3D7_0208500, aACP) that retains canonical ACP features.
source: Consistent with FASII targeting to the apicoplast in P. falciparum, this organelle features a well-studied ACP homolog (PF3D7_0208500, aACP) that retains canonical ACP features, including the conserved Ser modified by a 4-Ppant group required for FASII function (Shears et al., 2015; Gallagher and Prigge, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Apicoplast FASII activity is essential for P. falciparum growth within mosquitoes and the human liver.
source: Although apicoplast FASII activity is essential for P. falciparum growth within mosquitoes and the human liver, this pathway is dispensable for blood-stage parasites, which can scavenge fatty acids from the host (Shears et al., 2015; van Schaijk et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Apicoplast FASII is dispensable for blood-stage P. falciparum parasites, which can scavenge fatty acids from the host.
source: Although apicoplast FASII activity is essential for P. falciparum growth within mosquitoes and the human liver, this pathway is dispensable for blood-stage parasites, which can scavenge fatty acids from the host (Shears et al., 2015; van Schaijk et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: P. falciparum has retained a second ACP homolog (PF3D7_1208300) annotated as a mitochondrial ACP (mACP).
source: Despite loss of mitochondrial FASII enzymes, P. falciparum has curiously retained a second ACP homolog (PF3D7_1208300) that is annotated as a mitochondrial ACP (mACP) but has not been directly studied.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and sequence analysis.

claim: Genome-wide knock-out studies in Plasmodium berghei and P. falciparum reported that the mACP gene was refractory to disruption.
source: We noted that recent genome-wide knock-out studies in Plasmodium berghei and P. falciparum both reported that this gene was refractory to disruption, suggesting an essential, FASII-independent function (Zhang et al., 2018; Gomes et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Recent studies in yeast and human cells have identified an expanding network of mitochondrial ACP interactions beyond FASII that includes roles in respiratory chain assembly, Fe-S cluster biogenesis, and mitochondrial ribosomal translation.
source: Recent studies in yeast and human cells have identified an expanding network of mitochondrial ACP interactions beyond FASII that includes roles in respiratory chain assembly, Fe-S cluster biogenesis, and mitochondrial ribosomal translation (Van Vranken et al., 2016; Van Vranken et al., 2018; Nowinski et al., 2020; Brown et al., 2017; Majmudar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Critical mACP interactions in yeast and/or humans are linked to mitochondrial FASII function and the Ppant group of ACP.
source: However, in all cases these critical interactions in yeast and/or humans are linked to mitochondrial FASII function and the Ppant group of ACP (Brown et al., 2017; Cory et al., 2017; Angerer et al., 2014; Boniecki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: P. falciparum mACP localizes to the parasite mitochondrion.
source: We localized mACP to the P. falciparum mitochondrion and set out to understand its FASII-independent function in this organelle.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: P. falciparum mACP is essential for parasite viability.
source: Using conditional knockdown and immunoprecipitation (IP) studies, we discovered that mACP is essential for parasite viability and plays a critical role in binding and stabilizing the Isd11-Nfs1 cysteine desulfurase complex required for mitochondrial Fe-S cluster biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by the growth assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: P. falciparum mACP plays a critical role in binding and stabilizing the Isd11-Nfs1 cysteine desulfurase complex required for mitochondrial Fe-S cluster biogenesis.
source: Using conditional knockdown and immunoprecipitation (IP) studies, we discovered that mACP is essential for parasite viability and plays a critical role in binding and stabilizing the Isd11-Nfs1 cysteine desulfurase complex required for mitochondrial Fe-S cluster biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data (Figure 2D, 2F, 2G) and Western blot analysis showing loss of Nfs1 upon mACP knockdown (Figure 4A).

claim: P. falciparum mACP binds to Isd11 via a divergent molecular interface that does not involve a 4-Ppant group.
source: Unlike mACP interactions in yeast and humans, P. falciparum mACP binds to Isd11 via a divergent molecular interface that does not involve a 4-Ppant group.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis (Figure 1A) showing lack of conserved Ser, co-IP experiments (Figure 2D, 2F, 2G), and structural modeling (Figure 3B).

claim: P. falciparum mACP has replaced the conserved Ser with a Phe residue that cannot be modified by a 4-Ppant group.
source: Unlike the apicoplast ACP, which retains the conserved Ser for 4-Ppant attachment, mACP has curiously replaced this Ser with a Phe residue that cannot be modified by a 4-Ppant group (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Ser-to-Phe substitution in mACP is consistent with the loss of mitochondrial FASII and the ACP-modifying phosphopantetheine transferase enzyme.
source: This Ser-to-Phe substitution in mACP is consistent with the loss of mitochondrial FASII and the ACP-modifying phosphopantetheine transferase enzyme (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and suggested a non-canonical function for mACP.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence analysis and BLAST results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Immunofluorescence analysis of mACP-HA2 revealed strong colocalization between mACP-HA2 and the mitochondrial marker, HSP60.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of this mACP-HA2 line revealed strong colocalization between mACP-HA2 and the mitochondrial marker, HSP60 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Full-length mACP-HA2 has a predicted molecular mass ~21 kDa.
source: Full-length mACP-HA2 has a predicted molecular mass ~21 kDa, but SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and western blot (WB) analysis of immunoprecipitated mACP-HA2 indicated that this protein migrated with an apparent molecular mass ~15 kDa (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on calculation from the protein sequence.

claim: Immunoprecipitated mACP-HA2 from parasites migrated with an apparent molecular mass ~15 kDa.
source: Full-length mACP-HA2 has a predicted molecular mass ~21 kDa, but SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and western blot (WB) analysis of immunoprecipitated mACP-HA2 indicated that this protein migrated with an apparent molecular mass ~15 kDa (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: mACP is post-translationally processed upon mitochondrial import.
source: This lower size suggested that mACP was likely to be post-translationally processed upon mitochondrial import, which would be consistent with known processing of mitochondrial ACP in yeast and humans (Vögtle et al., 2009; Vaca Jacome et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the difference between predicted and observed molecular mass and is consistent with known processing in other organisms.

claim: Recombinant, full-length mACP-HA2 expressed in E. coli migrated with an apparent molecular mass close to 21 kDa.
source: The recombinant, full-length mACP-HA2 expressed in bacteria migrated with an apparent molecular mass close to 21 kDa, as expected.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Leu-51 is at or near the N-terminus of mature mACP in P. falciparum parasites.
source: This truncated mACP protein co-migrated by SDS-PAGE with mACP-HA2 expressed in parasites (Figure 1C), suggesting that Leu-51 is at or near the N-terminus of mature mACP in parasites.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-migration of truncated and parasite-expressed mACP shown in Figure 1C and MS data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Parasites grew indistinguishably ± aTc for the first 3 days in the mACP knockdown experiment.
source: Parasites grew indistinguishably ± aTc for the first 3 days. However, parasites grown without aTc displayed a major growth defect on day 4 in the third intraerythrocytic lifecycle (Figure 1E), similar to prior studies with this knockdown system (Ganesan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the growth assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Parasites grown without aTc displayed a major growth defect on day 4 in the third intraerythrocytic lifecycle.
source: Parasites grew indistinguishably ± aTc for the first 3 days. However, parasites grown without aTc displayed a major growth defect on day 4 in the third intraerythrocytic lifecycle (Figure 1E), similar to prior studies with this knockdown system (Ganesan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the growth assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Blood-smear analysis on day 5 indicated widespread parasite death in -aTc conditions.
source: Blood-smear analysis on day 5 indicated widespread parasite death (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: WB analysis of parasite samples harvested in the second cycle, after 3 days of growth -aTc, indicated robust knockdown of mACP expression relative to parasites grown +aTc.
source: WB analysis of parasite samples harvested in the second cycle, after 3 days of growth -aTc, indicated robust knockdown of mACP expression relative to parasites grown +aTc (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1E inset.

claim: Mitochondrial LYR proteins in yeast and human cells bear a conserved Leu-Tyr-Arg (LYR) sequence motif on their N-terminal helix.
source: Recent studies in yeast and human cells have revealed that mitochondrial ACP binds to a variety of small, three-helical adapter proteins that bear a conserved Leu-Tyr-Arg (LYR) sequence motif on their N-terminal helix (Majmudar et al., 2019; Angerer, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The Leu in the LYR motif mediates an intramolecular helical-helical contact.
source: The Leu mediates an intramolecular helical-helical contact while the Tyr and Arg side chains interact with conserved acidic residues on ACP (Cory et al., 2017; Boniecki et al., 2017; Herrera et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The Tyr and Arg side chains of the LYR motif interact with conserved acidic residues on ACP.
source: The Leu mediates an intramolecular helical-helical contact while the Tyr and Arg side chains interact with conserved acidic residues on ACP (Cory et al., 2017; Boniecki et al., 2017; Herrera et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: LYR-motif proteins mediate diverse mitochondrial processes that include respiratory chain assembly, Fe-S cluster biogenesis, and ribosomal translation.
source: These LYR-motif proteins mediate diverse mitochondrial processes that include respiratory chain assembly, Fe-S cluster biogenesis, and ribosomal translation (Van Vranken et al., 2016; Van Vranken et al., 2018; Brown et al., 2017; Angerer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: P. falciparum lacks identifiable homologs of LYR proteins that mediate respiratory chain assembly (LYRM3/NDUFB9, LYRM6/NDUFA6, LYRM7/MZM1, LYRM8/SDHAF1, ACN9/SDHAF3, and FMC1/C7orf55) or interactions with mitochondrial ribosomes (L0R8F8).
source: In contrast to other eukaryotes, P. falciparum lacked identifiable homologs of LYR proteins that mediate respiratory chain assembly (LYRM3/NDUFB9, LYRM6/NDUFA6, LYRM7/MZM1, LYRM8/SDHAF1, ACN9/SDHAF3, and FMC1/C7orf55) or interactions with mitochondrial ribosomes (L0R8F8).
evidence: This is supported by BLAST analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: P. falciparum has a clear homolog for Isd11 (PF3D7_1311000, e-value 3e-6).
source: However, we identified a clear homolog for Isd11 (PF3D7_1311000, e-value 3e-6), which functions in Fe-S cluster biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by BLAST analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Isd11 is the only LYR-protein homolog retained by P. falciparum parasites.
source: Our BLAST analysis suggested that Isd11 is the only LYR-protein homolog retained by parasites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by BLAST analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: P. falciparum Isd11 is 29% identical to human Isd11.
source: P. falciparum Isd11 is 29% identical to human Isd11 (also known as LYRM4), including conservation of the LYR sequence motif near the N-terminus (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: P. falciparum Isd11 retains conservation of the LYR sequence motif near the N-terminus.
source: P. falciparum Isd11 is 29% identical to human Isd11 (also known as LYRM4), including conservation of the LYR sequence motif near the N-terminus (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The parasite mACP retains the conserved Glu residues known to interact with the Tyr and Arg residues of the LYR motif on Isd11.
source: The parasite mACP retains the conserved Glu residues (5 and 11 amino acids C-terminal to the modified Ser in canonical ACPs) known to interact with the Tyr and Arg residues of the LYR motif on Isd11 at the mACP-Isd11 binding interface (Figure 1A; Cory et al., 2017; Boniecki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment in Figure 1A and citations to prior structural studies.

claim: In yeast and humans, Isd11 directly binds and stabilizes Nfs1, a mitochondrial cysteine desulfurase required for biogenesis of Fe-S clusters.
source: In yeast and humans, Isd11 directly binds and stabilizes Nfs1, a mitochondrial cysteine desulfurase required for biogenesis of Fe-S clusters (Wiedemann et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Mitochondrial ACP in yeast and humans directly binds Isd11 to stabilize the mACP-Isd11-Nfs1 complex.
source: Mitochondrial ACP in these organisms directly binds Isd11 to stabilize the mACP-Isd11-Nfs1 complex (Figure 2B), with loss of ACP and/or Isd11 resulting in Nfs1 instability and defective Fe-S cluster biogenesis (Van Vranken et al., 2016; Lill and Freibert, 2020; Herrera et al., 2018; Cai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Loss of ACP and/or Isd11 in yeast and humans results in Nfs1 instability and defective Fe-S cluster biogenesis.
source: Mitochondrial ACP in these organisms directly binds Isd11 to stabilize the mACP-Isd11-Nfs1 complex (Figure 2B), with loss of ACP and/or Isd11 resulting in Nfs1 instability and defective Fe-S cluster biogenesis (Van Vranken et al., 2016; Lill and Freibert, 2020; Herrera et al., 2018; Cai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: P. falciparum retains a mitochondrial Nfs1 homolog (PF3D7_0727200) that is predicted to be essential.
source: P. falciparum retains a mitochondrial Nfs1 homolog (PF3D7_0727200) that is predicted from genome-wide knock-out studies to be essential (Gomes et al., 2015; Gisselberg et al., 2013) but whose role in Fe-S cluster biogenesis has not been studied.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior genome-wide knockout studies.

claim: Nfs1 was highly enriched in the mACP-HA2 IP sample compared to the aACP-HA2 control sample in multiple independent pulldowns.
source: In multiple independent pulldowns, we identified Nfs1 as strongly enriched in the mACP-HA2 sample compared to a negative control sample (anti-HA IP of aACP-HA2) (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Isd11 peptides were not observed in mACP-HA2 IP/MS samples.
source: We did not observe peptides corresponding to Isd11 in mACP-HA2 IP/MS samples. However, its absence is not unexpected given the short Isd11 length (87 residues) that leads to comparatively few tryptic peptides.
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry analysis of IP samples.

claim: Isd11-GFP expressed in parasites colocalized with MitoTracker.
source: We confirmed that Isd11-GFP expressed in this line colocalized with MitoTracker (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Reciprocal IP/WB experiments confirmed stable interaction of mACP-HA2 and Isd11-GFP in parasites.
source: Using this Dd2 line expressing mACP-HA2 and Isd11-GFP, we performed reciprocal IP/WB experiments that confirmed stable interaction of these two proteins in parasites (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP/Western blot data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: mACP did not co-IP with the abundant mitochondrial chaperone, HSP60.
source: This interaction appeared to be specific as mACP did not co-IP with the abundant mitochondrial chaperone, HSP60, or with GFP-tagged cytochrome c1 (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP/Western blot data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: mACP did not co-IP with GFP-tagged cytochrome c1.
source: This interaction appeared to be specific as mACP did not co-IP with the abundant mitochondrial chaperone, HSP60, or with GFP-tagged cytochrome c1 (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP/Western blot data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Reciprocal IP experiments with lysates from bacteria coexpressing P. falciparum mACP-HA2 and Isd11-His6 confirmed stable interaction of these proteins in the absence of other parasite-specific factors.
source: Reciprocal IP experiments with lysates from bacteria coexpressing P. falciparum mACP-HA2 and Isd11-His6 confirmed stable interaction of these proteins in the absence of other parasite-specific factors (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP/Western blot data from E. coli shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The mACP-Isd11 interaction was strongly reduced (YR/AA) or eliminated (LYR/AAA) by Isd11 LYR mutations.
source: In experiments with Isd11 LYR mutants, however, this interaction was strongly reduced (YR/AA) or eliminated (LYR/AAA), despite similar expression of all recombinant proteins (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP/Western blot data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Analysis by Coomassie-stained SDS-PAGE and tandem MS indicated robust isolation of a 1:1 complex containing Isd11 and mACP.
source: Analysis by Coomassie-stained SDS-PAGE and tandem MS indicated robust isolation of a 1:1 complex containing Isd11 and mACP (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE data in Figure 2G and mass spectrometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: mACP directly binds to Isd11 and this interaction involves the LYR motif.
source: We conclude that mACP directly binds to Isd11 and that this interaction involves the LYR motif.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP experiments in E. coli (Figure 2F) and mutagenesis studies (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).

claim: Yeast and human Isd11 retain a conserved Arg-6 residues upstream of the LYR motif that electrostatically stabilizes the negatively charged oxygen atoms of the Ppant group in the ACP-Isd11 complex.
source: Yeast and human Isd11 retain a conserved Arg-6 residues upstream of the LYR motif (Figure 2A) that electrostatically stabilizes the negatively charged oxygen atoms of the Ppant group in the ACP-Isd11 complex (Cory et al., 2017; Boniecki et al., 2017; Herrera et al., 2019), and mutation of this Arg ablates binding of human Isd11 to ACP (Majmudar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural and biochemical studies.

claim: Mutation of Arg-6 in human Isd11 ablates binding to ACP.
source: Yeast and human Isd11 retain a conserved Arg-6 residues upstream of the LYR motif (Figure 2A) that electrostatically stabilizes the negatively charged oxygen atoms of the Ppant group in the ACP-Isd11 complex (Cory et al., 2017; Boniecki et al., 2017; Herrera et al., 2019), and mutation of this Arg ablates binding of human Isd11 to ACP (Majmudar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: P. falciparum Isd11 has replaced Arg-6 with an Ile residue.
source: The parasite Isd11, however, has replaced Arg-6 with an Ile residue (Figure 2A) expected to more favorably interact with the local hydrophobic surface of mACP created by Ser-to-Phe substitution.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Parasite Isd11 has co-evolved with mACP to optimize formation of the mACP-Isd11 complex in P. falciparum in the absence of FASII and an acyl-Ppant group on mACP.
source: These sequence features suggest that parasite Isd11 has co-evolved with mACP to optimize formation of the mACP-Isd11 complex in P. falciparum in the absence of FASII and an acyl-Ppant group on mACP.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence changes in both mACP (Ser to Phe) and Isd11 (Arg to Ile) that are complementary.

claim: Recombinant parasite Isd11 expressed in bacteria did not co-purify with the endogenous ~9 kDa E. coli ACP.
source: Consistent with this model, recombinantly parasite Isd11 expressed in bacteria did not co-purify with the endogenous ~9 kDa E. coli ACP (Figure 2G) or with coexpressed apicoplast ACP (Figure 2—figure supplement 7), both of which retain the conserved Ser and Ppant modification.
evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Recombinant parasite Isd11 expressed in bacteria did not co-purify with coexpressed apicoplast ACP.
source: Consistent with this model, recombinantly parasite Isd11 expressed in bacteria did not co-purify with the endogenous ~9 kDa E. coli ACP (Figure 2G) or with coexpressed apicoplast ACP (Figure 2—figure supplement 7), both of which retain the conserved Ser and Ppant modification.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: Human Isd11 robustly binds bacterial ACP when expressed in E. coli.
source: This specificity by P. falciparum Isd11 contrasts with that of human Isd11, which robustly binds bacterial ACP when expressed in E. coli (Cory et al., 2017; Boniecki et al., 2017; Cai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Association of Isd11 and mACP in yeast and human cells depends critically on the acyl-Ppant group of mACP.
source: Association of Isd11 and mACP in yeast and human cells depends critically on the acyl-Ppant group of mACP (Figure 3A), with little or no association observed in these cells between Isd11 and the mACP Ser-to-Ala mutant that lacks a Ppant group (Van Vranken et al., 2016; Van Vranken et al., 2018; Majmudar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Little or no association is observed in yeast and human cells between Isd11 and the mACP Ser-to-Ala mutant that lacks a Ppant group.
source: Association of Isd11 and mACP in yeast and human cells depends critically on the acyl-Ppant group of mACP (Figure 3A), with little or no association observed in these cells between Isd11 and the mACP Ser-to-Ala mutant that lacks a Ppant group (Van Vranken et al., 2016; Van Vranken et al., 2018; Majmudar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The mACP-Isd11 interface in yeast and humans includes key electrostatic interactions between conserved Lys and Arg residues in Isd11 and Glu and Asp residues in mACP.
source: The mACP-Isd11 interface in these organisms also includes key electrostatic interactions between conserved Lys and Arg residues in Isd11 and Glu and Asp residues in mACP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Cory et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural studies and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Rosetta structural model suggests that the unusual Phe113 residue of mACP partitions into a hydrophobic pocket at the mACP-Isd11 interface.
source: The resulting low-energy structural model suggested that the unusual Phe113 residue of mACP partitions into a hydrophobic pocket at the mACP-Isd11 interface composed of the aliphatic side-chain methylene groups of Lys10 and Arg14 and the phenyl ring of Tyr13 of Isd11 as well as Val117 on mACP (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on computational structural modeling shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The predicted mACP-Isd11 binding interface includes conserved electrostatic interactions between basic residues on parasite Isd11 and acidic groups on mACP.
source: The predicted binding interface also included conserved electrostatic interactions between basic residues on parasite Isd11 and acidic groups on mACP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on computational structural modeling shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: WT mACP-HA2 but not the F113A mutant co-purified with Isd11 in Ni-NTA pulldown experiments from E. coli.
source: We then used Ni-NTA to selectively pull down His-tagged Isd11 and observed that WT mACP-HA2 but not the F113A mutant co-purified with Isd11 (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutation of Phe113 to Ala substantially weakens the mACP-Isd11 interaction.
source: These results indicate that mutation of Phe113 to Ala substantially weakens the mACP-Isd11 interaction, supporting the conclusion that Phe113 contributes to the mACP-Isd11 binding interface in the mACP-Isd11-Nfs1 complex as suggested by structural modeling (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of co-purification in the F113A mutant shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Parasites expressing a second copy of WT mACP showed identical growth in the presence or absence of aTc.
source: Parasites expressing a second copy of WT mACP showed identical growth in the presence or absence of aTc. In contrast, parasites that episomally expressed the F113A mACP mutant showed strongly diminished growth upon aTc removal and loss of endogenous mACP (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Parasites that episomally expressed the F113A mACP mutant showed strongly diminished growth upon aTc removal and loss of endogenous mACP.
source: Parasites expressing a second copy of WT mACP showed identical growth in the presence or absence of aTc. In contrast, parasites that episomally expressed the F113A mACP mutant showed strongly diminished growth upon aTc removal and loss of endogenous mACP (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The Phe residue of mACP plays a key role in stabilizing the mACP-Isd11 association required for Nfs1 stability and function.
source: These results support the conclusion that the Phe residue of mACP plays a key role in stabilizing the mACP-Isd11 association required for Nfs1 stability and function.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability of the F113A mutant to rescue parasite growth upon endogenous mACP knockdown (Figure 3D).

claim: Nfs1 stability in other eukaryotes depends critically on its association with Isd11 and ACP.
source: Nfs1 stability in other eukaryotes depends critically on its association with Isd11 and ACP, with loss of ACP resulting in degradation of Nfs1 and lethal defects in Fe-S cluster biogenesis (Van Vranken et al., 2016; Cory et al., 2017; Boniecki et al., 2017; Lill and Freibert, 2020; Cai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Loss of ACP in other eukaryotes results in degradation of Nfs1 and lethal defects in Fe-S cluster biogenesis.
source: Nfs1 stability in other eukaryotes depends critically on its association with Isd11 and ACP, with loss of ACP resulting in degradation of Nfs1 and lethal defects in Fe-S cluster biogenesis (Van Vranken et al., 2016; Cory et al., 2017; Boniecki et al., 2017; Lill and Freibert, 2020; Cai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The commercial anti-Nfs1 antibody (Abcam 229829) selectively recognized recombinant P. falciparum Nfs1 expressed in E. coli.
source: To test the impact of mACP knockdown on Nfs1 protein levels in parasites, we used a commercial anti-Nfs1 antibody (Abcam 229829) raised against a 250-amino acid region of human Nfs1 that is 55% identical to P. falciparum Nfs1 and that selectively recognized recombinant P. falciparum Nfs1 expressed in E. coli (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In parasites grown +aTc, the anti-Nfs1 antibody recognized a band at ~60 kDa.
source: In parasites grown +aTc, the anti-Nfs1 antibody recognized a band at ~60 kDa (Figure 4A) that is close to the predicted molecular mass of 63 kDa for this protein.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: WB analysis of parasites grown in -aTc conditions failed to detect the ~60 kDa Nfs1 band.
source: WB analysis of parasites grown in -aTc conditions failed to detect this ~60 kDa band (Figure 4A), strongly suggesting that Nfs1 stability is tightly coupled to mACP expression and that loss of mACP results in Nfs1 degradation in parasites as it does in yeast (Van Vranken et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Nfs1 stability is tightly coupled to mACP expression in P. falciparum.
source: WB analysis of parasites grown in -aTc conditions failed to detect this ~60 kDa band (Figure 4A), strongly suggesting that Nfs1 stability is tightly coupled to mACP expression and that loss of mACP results in Nfs1 degradation in parasites as it does in yeast (Van Vranken et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of Nfs1 signal upon mACP knockdown shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Loss of mACP results in Nfs1 degradation in P. falciparum parasites.
source: WB analysis of parasites grown in -aTc conditions failed to detect this ~60 kDa band (Figure 4A), strongly suggesting that Nfs1 stability is tightly coupled to mACP expression and that loss of mACP results in Nfs1 degradation in parasites as it does in yeast (Van Vranken et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of Nfs1 signal upon mACP knockdown shown in Figure 4A and is consistent with prior work in yeast.

claim: The epitope-tagged Rieske band was detected ~43 kDa in WB analysis of parasites grown + aTc.
source: A band corresponding to the epitope-tagged Rieske was detected ~43 kDa in WB analysis of parasites grown + aTc. This band, however, was undetectable in parasites grown 72 hr in -aTc conditions to downregulate mACP expression (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Rieske band was undetectable in parasites grown 72 hr in -aTc conditions to downregulate mACP expression.
source: A band corresponding to the epitope-tagged Rieske was detected ~43 kDa in WB analysis of parasites grown + aTc. This band, however, was undetectable in parasites grown 72 hr in -aTc conditions to downregulate mACP expression (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Knockdown of mACP and subsequent degradation of Nfs1 are accompanied by loss of the Fe-S cluster-dependent Rieske protein.
source: These results indicate that knockdown of mACP and subsequent degradation of Nfs1 are accompanied by loss of the Fe-S cluster-dependent Rieske protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the Western blot data showing loss of both Nfs1 and Rieske upon mACP knockdown (Figure 4A, 4B).

claim: Loss of mACP in -aTc conditions did not reduce expression levels of the mitochondrial chaperone HSP60.
source: The impact of mACP knockdown on stability of Nfs1 and Rieske was specific to these proteins as loss of mACP in -aTc conditions did not reduce expression levels of the mitochondrial chaperone HSP60 or the integral ETC complex III component, cyt c1 (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Loss of mACP in -aTc conditions did not reduce expression levels of the integral ETC complex III component, cyt c1.
source: The impact of mACP knockdown on stability of Nfs1 and Rieske was specific to these proteins as loss of mACP in -aTc conditions did not reduce expression levels of the mitochondrial chaperone HSP60 or the integral ETC complex III component, cyt c1 (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Rieske protein is an essential electron-transfer component of ETC complex III.
source: Since the Rieske protein is an essential electron-transfer component of ETC complex III (Zhang et al., 1998), we reasoned that loss of mACP and Rieske likely results in ETC failure.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: In blood-stage parasites, the essential function of the mitochondrial ETC is to oxidatively recycle the ubiquinone cofactor used by several dehydrogenases, of which dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHOD) is most critical.
source: In blood-stage parasites, which rely on glycolysis rather than oxidative phosphorylation for ATP synthesis, the essential function of the mitochondrial ETC is to oxidatively recycle the ubiquinone cofactor used by several dehydrogenases, of which dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHOD) is most critical (Painter et al., 2007; Ke et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Exogenous addition of decyl-ubiquinone (dQ) rescues parasites from ETC dysfunction caused by the ETC complex III inhibitor, atovaquone.
source: Prior work has shown that exogenous addition of the soluble ubiquinone analog, decyl-ubiquinone (dQ), rescues parasites from ETC dysfunction caused by the ETC complex III inhibitor, atovaquone (Ke et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: 15 µM exogenous dQ substantially rescued parasites over multiple intraerythrocytic cycles from growth inhibition by 100 nM atovaquone.
source: As a positive control and to provide a basis for comparison, we first confirmed that 15 µM exogenous dQ substantially rescued parasites over multiple intraerythrocytic cycles from growth inhibition by 100 nM atovaquone (Figure 5A), as previously reported (Ke et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Parasites cultured -aTc grew normally for 3 days but failed to expand into the third growth cycle on day 4.
source: As before, -aTc parasites grew normally for 3 days but failed to expand into the third growth cycle on day 4 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Addition of dQ rescued parasite growth in the third growth cycle in -aTc conditions.
source: Addition of dQ rescued parasite growth in the third growth cycle in -aTc conditions, similar to dQ rescue of parasites from atovaquone.
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: dQ only rescued the third-cycle growth of parasites cultured -aTc, which failed to expand further and began to die off on day 6 in the fourth intraerythrocytic cycle.
source: However, in contrast to indefinite parasite rescue from atovaquone, dQ only rescued the third-cycle growth of parasites cultured -aTc, which failed to expand further and began to die off on day 6 in the fourth intraerythrocytic cycle (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ETC failure is the immediate cause of parasite death upon mACP knockdown.
source: On the basis of dQ rescue, we conclude that ETC failure is the immediate cause of parasite death upon mACP knockdown.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of dQ to rescue parasites in the third cycle shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Additional dysfunctions beyond the mitochondrial ETC contribute to parasite death on a longer timescale upon mACP knockdown.
source: However, the inability of dQ to rescue parasites beyond the third cycle indicates that additional dysfunctions beyond the mitochondrial ETC contribute to parasite death on a longer timescale.
evidence: This is inferred from the failure of dQ to rescue parasites beyond the third cycle shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The ETC couples ubiquinone recycling to proton translocation from the mitochondrial matrix to the inner membrane space to establish a transmembrane electrochemical potential.
source: The ETC couples ubiquinone recycling to proton translocation from the mitochondrial matrix to the inner membrane space to establish a transmembrane electrochemical potential.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ETC function.

claim: Parasites retain a second proton-pumping mechanism that also contributes to transmembrane potential and that is inhibited by proguanil.
source: Prior work has shown that parasites retain a second proton-pumping mechanism that also contributes to transmembrane potential and that is inhibited by proguanil (Painter et al., 2007; Skinner-Adams et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Inhibition of ETC function kills parasites due to defective ubiquinone recycling but does not substantially depolarize mitochondria due to activity by the proguanil-sensitive pathway.
source: Inhibition of ETC function kills parasites due to defective ubiquinone recycling but does not substantially depolarize mitochondria due to activity by this second, proguanil-sensitive pathway.
evidence: This is based on prior published work cited in the manuscript.

claim: ETC dysfunction plus proguanil treatment blocks both pathways for proton pumping and causes mitochondrial depolarization.
source: However, ETC dysfunction plus proguanil treatment blocks both pathways for proton pumping and causes mitochondrial depolarization, which can be visualized by a failure to concentrate charged dyes like MitoTracker within the mitochondrion that leads to dispersed dye accumulation in the cytoplasm (Painter et al., 2007; Ke et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Parasite treatment with sublethal proguanil negated the ability of dQ to rescue parasite growth from mACP knockdown in the third cycle.
source: We repeated the prior growth assay ± aTc and ±dQ but also included 1 µM proguanil. This proguanil concentration alone had no effect on parasite growth, as previously reported (Painter et al., 2007). However, when proguanil was combined with growth -aTc, dQ was unable to rescue parasite growth in the third cycle (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Proguanil treatment selectively prevented mitochondrial accumulation of MitoTracker Red in parasites grown -aTc.
source: Microscopy analysis of parasites on day 3 of the growth assay revealed that proguanil treatment selectively prevented mitochondrial accumulation of MitoTracker Red in parasites grown -aTc, strongly suggesting mitochondrial depolarization (Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5C, 5D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Impaired ubiquinone recycling due to Rieske loss and ETC dysfunction is the immediate cause of parasite death upon mACP knockdown.
source: This observation strongly supports the model that impaired ubiquinone recycling due to Rieske loss and ETC dysfunction is the immediate cause of parasite death upon mACP knockdown.
evidence: This is inferred from the dQ rescue and mitochondrial depolarization experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The P. falciparum mitochondrion is a major antimalarial drug target.
source: The P. falciparum mitochondrion is a major antimalarial drug target, but nearly all organelle-specific inhibitors target cytochrome b in ETC complex III or DHOD that depends on complex III function (Antonova-Koch et al., 2018; Goodman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Nearly all organelle-specific inhibitors target cytochrome b in ETC complex III or DHOD that depends on complex III function.
source: The P. falciparum mitochondrion is a major antimalarial drug target, but nearly all organelle-specific inhibitors target cytochrome b in ETC complex III or DHOD that depends on complex III function (Antonova-Koch et al., 2018; Goodman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Many mitochondrial metabolic pathways are dispensable for blood-stage parasites.
source: Multiple metabolic pathways operate within the mitochondrion (van Dooren et al., 2006), but many are dispensable for blood-stage parasites, and few essential blood-stage functions beyond DHOD and ETC complexes III and IV have been identified.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work and represents established knowledge.

claim: ISC biosynthesis is an ancient, essential mitochondrial function that has been well studied in yeast and mammalian cells but is sparsely studied in parasites.
source: ISC biosynthesis is an ancient, essential mitochondrial function that has been well studied in yeast and mammalian cells but is sparsely studied in parasites (Gisselberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work and represents established knowledge.

claim: Most eukaryotic cells retain a mitochondrial FASII pathway in which the acyl-ACP intermediate critically mediates respiratory chain assembly, Fe-S cluster biogenesis, and ribosomal translation by binding to LYR-protein assembly factors.
source: Most eukaryotic cells, including fungi, plants, and animals, retain a mitochondrial FASII pathway in which the acyl-ACP intermediate has been shown to critically mediate respiratory chain assembly, Fe-S cluster biogenesis, and ribosomal translation by binding to LYR-protein assembly factors (Majmudar et al., 2019; Angerer, 2015; Nowinski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: ACP interactions with LYR proteins and their dependence on ACP acylation have been proposed to constitute a regulatory feedback mechanism that couples the availability of acetyl-CoA for FASII activity to respiratory chain assembly for oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthesis.
source: These interactions and their dependence on ACP acylation have been proposed to constitute a regulatory feedback mechanism that couples the availability of acetyl-CoA for FASII activity to respiratory chain assembly for oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthesis (Van Vranken et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Biochemical coupling of FASII and respiratory chain assembly has not been retained in Plasmodium.
source: Biochemical coupling of these pathways, however, has not been retained in Plasmodium, which has lost mitochondrial FASII enzymes but retains a divergent ACP homolog incapable of 4-Ppant modification or acylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of mitochondrial FASII enzymes and the Ser-to-Phe substitution in mACP.

claim: mACP remains essential to parasites for Fe-S cluster biogenesis by binding to Isd11.
source: Nevertheless, we have shown that mACP remains essential to parasites for Fe-S cluster biogenesis by binding to Isd11, which is the only LYR-protein homolog retained by P. falciparum.
evidence: This is supported by the growth assay data (Figure 1E), co-IP experiments (Figure 2D, 2F, 2G), and loss of Nfs1 upon mACP knockdown (Figure 4A).

claim: Isd11 binds to mACP via a novel molecular interface.
source: Isd11 binds to mACP via a novel interface molecular interface, and this interaction is critical stabilizing the mACP-Isd11-Nfs1 cysteine desulfurase complex.
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling (Figure 3B) and mutagenesis studies (Figure 3C, 3D).

claim: P. falciparum provides a new molecular paradigm for essential ACP function without an acyl-Ppant group.
source: P. falciparum thus provides a new molecular paradigm for essential ACP function without an acyl-Ppant group.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective findings showing mACP essentiality and function without a Ppant group.

claim: Prior in vitro work has provided evidence that activity of purified Isd11-Nfs1 does not strictly require association with ACP.
source: Prior in vitro work has provided evidence that activity of purified Isd11-Nfs1 does not strictly require association with ACP (Boniecki et al., 2017; Lill and Freibert, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Nfs1 is unstable in its native mitochondrial context in the absence of ACP in P. falciparum and yeast.
source: However, Nfs1 is unstable in its native mitochondrial context in the absence of ACP, as shown herein for P. falciparum and in prior studies of yeast (Van Vranken et al., 2016; Adam et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing loss of Nfs1 upon mACP knockdown (Figure 4A) and citations to prior work in yeast.

claim: Coupling Nfs1 stability (via Isd11) to ACP acylation in eukaryotes that retain mitochondrial FASII has been proposed as a mechanism to up- and downregulate Fe-S cluster biogenesis congruent with nutrient availability and cellular Fe-S cluster needs.
source: Coupling Nfs1 stability (via Isd11) to ACP acylation in eukaryotes that retain mitochondrial FASII has been proposed as a mechanism to up- and downregulate Fe-S cluster biogenesis congruent with nutrient availability and cellular Fe-S cluster needs for respiration and growth (Lill and Freibert, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: The regulatory mechanism coupling Nfs1 stability to ACP acylation cannot explain mitochondrial retention of an acylation-incompetent ACP homolog in Plasmodium.
source: This mechanism, however, cannot explain mitochondrial retention of an acylation-incompetent ACP homolog in Plasmodium.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that parasite mACP lacks the Ser required for Ppant modification and acylation.

claim: ACP may play additional functional and/or regulatory roles that are essential for mitochondrial Fe-S cluster biogenesis and utilization in cells.
source: ACP may therefore play additional functional and/or regulatory roles that are essential for mitochondrial Fe-S cluster biogenesis and utilization in cells, perhaps involving metal-ion binding and sensing by ACP (e.g., iron or zinc) (Herrera et al., 2019; Qiu and Janson, 2004) or interactions with other mitochondrial networks akin to broad ACP interactions observed in E. coli (Gully et al., 2003).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the retention of mACP without acylation function and citations to prior work.

claim: Anaerobic eukaryotic parasites like Giardia and Cryptosporidium lack a mitochondrion but retain a primitive mitosome for Fe-S cluster biogenesis that lacks ACP and Isd11 homologs.
source: In this regard, it is interesting to note that anaerobic eukaryotic parasites like Giardia and Cryptosporidium lack a mitochondrion but retain a primitive mitosome for Fe-S cluster biogenesis that lacks ACP and Isd11 homologs in this compartment, where Nfs1 appears to function autonomously (Richards and van der Giezen, 2006; Braymer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Loss of mitochondrial FASII, but retention of a Ppant-independent mACP lacking the conserved Ser, appears to be widespread among apicomplexan parasites, including Toxoplasma and Babesia.
source: Loss of mitochondrial FASII, but retention of a Ppant-independent mACP lacking the conserved Ser, appears to be widespread among apicomplexan parasites, including Toxoplasma and Babesia (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: T. gondii has two divergent mACP homologs (TGME49_270310 and TGME49_265538), differing in the presence of a Cys or Gly in place of the conserved Ser.
source: In the case of Toxoplasma gondii, BLAST analysis revealed two divergent mACP homologs (TGME49_270310 and TGME49_265538), differing in the presence of a Cys or Gly in place of the conserved Ser, in their transcriptional profiles, and in their predicted contribution to parasite infection of human fibroblasts (Sidik et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by BLAST analysis and citation to prior published work.

claim: The chromerid Vitrella brassicaformis has a divergent ACP lacking the conserved Ser, but its algal cousin Chromera velia does not.
source: Outside the phylum Apicomplexa, the only genomic evidence we found for a divergent ACP lacking the conserved Ser was in the related photosynthetic chromerid, Vitrella brassicaformis, but not in its algal cousin, Chromera velia (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The adaptation of mitochondrial ACP to function without a Ppant group or acylation likely occurred on a similar evolutionary timeframe as the loss of plastid photosynthesis that accompanied the appearance of apicomplexan parasitism.
source: Thus, the adaptation of mitochondrial ACP to function without a Ppant group or acylation likely occurred on a similar evolutionary timeframe as the loss of plastid photosynthesis that accompanied the appearance of apicomplexan parasitism (Janouškovec et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of divergent mACP and citation to prior work on apicomplexan evolution.

claim: Mitochondrial ACP function without an acyl-Ppant group is a parasite-specific adaptation that differentiates apicomplexan parasites from humans.
source: Our study indicates that mitochondrial ACP function without an acyl-Ppant group is a parasite-specific adaptation that differentiates apicomplexan parasites from humans.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective findings and comparison with human mACP function.

claim: Loss of ACP destabilizes Nfs1 to block Fe-S cluster assembly, impairs the stability and function of the Rieske subunit of ETC complex III, and leads to parasite death.
source: Nevertheless, like yeast and human cells (Van Vranken et al., 2016; Majmudar et al., 2019), we observed that loss of ACP destabilizes Nfs1 to block Fe-S cluster assembly impairs the stability and function of the key Rieske subunit of ETC complex III and leads to parasite death (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data (Figure 4A, 4B) and growth assays (Figure 1E, Figure 5).

claim: In yeast and mammalian cells, mACP plays a second role in Rieske maturation by binding to MZM1, an LYR-protein chaperone.
source: In yeast and mammalian cells, mACP plays a second role in Rieske maturation by binding to MZM1, an LYR-protein chaperone that stabilizes Rieske upon import into the mitochondrial matrix to receive its Fe-S cluster for subsequent insertion into ETC complex III by the AAA-ATPase, BCS1 (Majmudar et al., 2019; Atkinson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: P. falciparum appears to lack an MZM1 homolog.
source: P. falciparum, however, appears to lack an MZM1 homolog (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that parasites have evolved compensatory mechanisms for Rieske maturation in the absence of this ACP-dependent chaperone.
evidence: This is supported by BLAST analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Parasites have evolved compensatory mechanisms for Rieske maturation in the absence of the ACP-dependent chaperone MZM1.
source: P. falciparum, however, appears to lack an MZM1 homolog (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that parasites have evolved compensatory mechanisms for Rieske maturation in the absence of this ACP-dependent chaperone.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of MZM1 homolog but retention of Rieske function.

claim: In yeast, loss of mACP and/or the Rieske protein results in accumulation of a late core assembly intermediate of complex III that contains cyt b, cyt c1, and other factors.
source: In yeast, loss of mACP and/or the Rieske protein, which is a peripheral subunit inserted late in the assembly of ETC complex III, results in accumulation of a late core assembly intermediate of complex III that contains cyt b, cyt c1, and other factors (Van Vranken et al., 2016; Atkinson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Cyt c1 levels are retained upon loss of parasite mACP and Rieske in -aTc conditions.
source: Our observation that cyt c1 levels are retained upon loss of parasite mACP and Rieske in -aTc conditions (Figure 4) suggests that this late complex III assembly intermediate likely accumulates in P. falciparum similar to yeast.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A late complex III assembly intermediate likely accumulates in P. falciparum upon mACP loss, similar to yeast.
source: Our observation that cyt c1 levels are retained upon loss of parasite mACP and Rieske in -aTc conditions (Figure 4) suggests that this late complex III assembly intermediate likely accumulates in P. falciparum similar to yeast.
evidence: This is inferred from the retention of cyt c1 levels upon mACP knockdown (Figure 4C) and comparison with yeast.

claim: Exogenous dQ rescued parasite growth upon mACP knockdown for one intraerythrocytic cycle but did not rescue growth on a longer timescale.
source: Exogenous dQ rescued parasite growth upon mACP knockdown for one intraerythrocytic cycle but did not rescue growth on a longer timescale.
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Respiratory failure is the immediate cause of P. falciparum death upon loss of mACP.
source: This short-term rescue indicates that respiratory failure is the immediate cause of P. falciparum death upon loss of mACP (Painter et al., 2007; Ke et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the dQ rescue data shown in Figure 5A and citations to prior work.

claim: Defects in essential processes beyond the mitochondrial ETC contribute to parasite death on longer timescales upon mACP knockdown.
source: However, defects in essential processes beyond the mitochondrial ETC contribute to parasite death on longer timescales.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability of dQ to rescue parasites beyond the third cycle shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Defects beyond the mitochondrial ETC may involve mitochondrial fumarate hydratase and/or essential Fe-S cluster proteins in the cytosol and nucleus that depend on Nfs1 activity.
